prompt: Why does the lesson call “fine” the correct reply to “how’s it going?”
hint: What kind of question is it?

choices.text: People always lie to their managers
choices.why: The lesson says “fine” is not a lie; it is an honest summary of a vague question.

choices.text: Things usually are fine
choices.why: Sometimes they are, but that is not why the reply is correct; it would be the same answer either way.

choices.text: Engineers prefer short answers in meetings
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson is about engineers’ preferences.

choices.text: The question is a greeting with no edges, and “fine” is its standard reply
choices.why: Right: nobody has been asked anything yet, so a summary is an accurate answer.

prompt: Which of the three reasons for “fine” does not go away with better wording?

choices.text: The question is a greeting
choices.why: Better wording turns the greeting into a real question.

choices.text: The question has no edges
choices.why: Edges are exactly what better wording adds.

choices.text: The manager’s power
choices.why: Right: the power is real even when the manager is kind, and wording cannot remove it.

choices.text: The meeting is too short to say anything that matters, however the question is phrased
choices.why: Not one of the three reasons; the lesson’s third reason is the manager’s power.

prompt: Thiago said on-call was fine. What did “fine” describe, and what did it leave out?
hint: Pages were answered and incidents resolved.

choices.text: Nothing true; he was hiding a failure
choices.why: Nothing he said was false; incidents were resolved.

choices.text: The team’s on-call, and left out his own week, which had gone badly in every respect
choices.why: His own pages were answered; what was missing was the cost, not a failed week.

choices.text: His feelings, and left out the facts
choices.why: It was the other way round: the facts were there and the cost was missing.

choices.text: The outcome, which was working, and left out what that outcome was costing him every week
choices.why: Right: on-call was functioning; the sleepless nights and the unexplained alert were the cost nobody asked about.

prompt: Which three things does the lesson say a manager controls and the person does not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Before, during and after the answer.

choices.text: Whether there is a problem to raise
choices.why: No: the manager controls how easy it is to raise one, not whether one exists.

choices.text: What happens afterwards
choices.why: Yes: lesson 7 is about it.

choices.text: The reaction to the answer
choices.why: Yes: a bad reaction teaches the person not to raise things.

choices.text: How open the person is by nature
choices.why: No: the lesson rejects putting the work on the person’s openness.

choices.text: The question
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: Which question has edges, in the lesson’s sense?
hint: Something to search for rather than to summarise.

choices.text: “How are things?”
choices.why: No edges at all; it invites a summary.

choices.text: “Is everything OK with you?”
choices.why: A yes-or-no question with nothing to search for.

choices.text: “Anything you want to tell me about work, home, the team, the product or your career?”
choices.why: A long list is still no edge; the person answers the easiest one, or none.

choices.text: “What was the most frustrating part of last week?”
choices.why: Right: a week, and “most”, give the person something specific to look for.

prompt: In a scaled question, which part does the lesson say does the work?

choices.text: The follow-up: what would make it one higher
choices.why: Right: the number alone says little; the follow-up asks for something small and concrete.

choices.text: The number, which can be compared across the team every week to spot trends early
choices.why: People use the scale differently, so numbers do not compare well across people.

choices.text: Choosing a scale of ten rather than five
choices.why: The size of the scale is not what the lesson discusses.

choices.text: Asking it at the start of the meeting
choices.why: Placement is not the point; the follow-up is.

prompt: Match each question that closes a conversation with what is wrong with it.

pairs.right: heard as an accusation even when it is curiosity
the only answer is the one inside it

pairs.left: “Have you thought about pairing with Diego?”
pairs.right: a suggestion wearing a question mark

pairs.left: “How’s on-call, and the calendar work, and the new process?”
pairs.right: the person answers the easiest one

prompt: Why does the lesson suggest asking about the team rather than the person, sometimes?

choices.text: To find out who is causing problems on the team
choices.why: It is not a way to collect information about colleagues.

choices.text: Because personal questions are inappropriate at work
choices.why: Several questions in the bank are personal, offered carefully.

choices.text: Because team problems matter more than individual ones in a company of ninety engineers
choices.why: The lesson does not rank them; it is about making a problem easier to raise.

choices.text: Some people find it easier to report a problem as everybody’s
choices.why: Right: the answer often turns out to be their own, and the question gave them a way in.

prompt: A manager asks, “What’s one thing I could do differently that would help you?” and gets “Nothing, you’re great.” What does the lesson suggest?
hint: The hardest question to answer honestly.

choices.text: Stop asking, since the answer was clear
choices.why: One answer to the hardest question is not a verdict.

choices.text: Insist until the person names something
choices.why: Insisting makes it a demand, which is the opposite of an easy way in.

choices.text: Ask the person’s colleagues instead
choices.why: That goes around the person and is not in the lesson.

choices.text: Keep asking regularly, and expect honest answers after a few months
choices.why: Right: the power gap makes this the hardest question, and honest answers come with time and repetition.

prompt: Thiago mentions the confusing alert. Renata replies, “I’ll get Diego to write a runbook.” Which of the three conversation-enders is that?

choices.text: Fixing
choices.why: Right: it closes the topic before the sleep and the reluctance to speak have come out.

choices.text: Explaining why on-call is hard for everybody at first
choices.why: That is explaining; here she offered a fix.

choices.text: Moving on
choices.why: She engaged with it; moving on would be “OK, good to know”.

choices.text: Saying it back
choices.why: Saying it back is one of the habits that keep the conversation open.

prompt: Put the response the lesson recommends to hard feedback about you in order.
items: Ask one question to understand it
Say what you will do with it
Explain, if needed, about a week later
trap: Explaining first is the natural reaction, and it teaches the person not to say such things again.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer “tell me more” to a specific follow-up at first?
hint: Whose guess does a specific follow-up carry?

choices.text: It is quicker
choices.why: It is not about speed.

choices.text: Specific questions are against the lesson’s rules
choices.why: The previous section is all about specific questions; the order matters here.

choices.text: It steers the person towards the manager’s guess
choices.why: Right: an open prompt carries no assumption about where the answer should go.

choices.text: Because people answer open prompts with shorter answers, which keeps the meeting on time
choices.why: The aim is the second and third answer, not a shorter meeting.

prompt: Renata summarises: “So the alert was confusing, and the worse part was not knowing who to call.” Thiago says, “Not exactly, I didn’t want to wake anybody.” What did saying it back achieve?

choices.text: It showed she was right all along
choices.why: He corrected her, which is the point of saying it back.

choices.text: It ended the topic politely so the meeting could move on to the next item on the agenda
choices.why: Saying it back keeps the topic open.

choices.text: Nothing; summaries waste time
choices.why: The correction is what it bought.

choices.text: A chance to correct her
choices.why: Right: the correction is the real problem, which a fix for the alert would have missed.

prompt: After the first answer, Renata waits by counting to ___ in her head.
hint: A few seconds longer than feels comfortable.

prompt: An engineer says in a one-to-one: “The new deploy process is fine, I guess.” Which reply follows the lesson best?

choices.text: “Great, glad it’s working. Next topic?”
choices.why: Moving on, after a “fine” with a hedge on the end.

choices.text: “What annoyed you most about it last week?”
choices.why: Right: a question with edges, asking for an event, with no fix and no explanation yet.

choices.text: “It takes some getting used to; everybody struggled with the old one too.”
choices.why: Explaining, which tells her the problem was already known.

choices.text: “Why do you only guess? Is something wrong with it?”
choices.why: A “why” about her choice of words, heard as an accusation.
